what_its_for: Levofloxacin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, sinus infections, urinary tract infections (UTIs), kidney infections, skin infections, and certain cases of anthrax or plague. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It will NOT work for colds, flu, or other viral infections.
how_to_take: Take levofloxacin by mouth once a day, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water (8 ounces). Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day while taking this medicine. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Take the full course of antibiotics even if you start feeling better — stopping early can let bacteria grow back and become harder to treat.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the dose that is right for your infection. Common doses range from 250 mg to 750 mg once daily. The length of treatment is usually 3 to 14 days depending on the type and severity of your infection. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store levofloxacin tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the tablets away from heat, light, and moisture. Do NOT store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. If you have leftover antibiotics, ask your pharmacist about safe disposal — do not flush them down the toilet or throw them in the trash.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids, vitamins, or supplements containing aluminum, magnesium, calcium, iron, or zinc within 2 hours before or 2 hours after taking levofloxacin, as they can prevent the medicine from working properly. Avoid excessive sun or UV light exposure — levofloxacin can make your skin much more sensitive to sunburn. Use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it may cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Avoid strenuous physical activity, as this medicine can rarely cause tendon problems. Do not drink alcohol excessively while taking this medication.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency care right away if you experience: sudden or worsening tendon pain, swelling, or snapping sensation (especially in the heel, shoulder, or wrist); chest pain, irregular heartbeat, or fainting; severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; tingling, numbness, or weakness in your arms or legs; confusion, memory problems, or hallucinations; diarrhea that is severe, watery, or bloody (even weeks after finishing the medicine); signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat. Also let your doctor know if your infection does not improve within a few days.
when_it_works: Many people start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting levofloxacin. However, it is very important to finish ALL of your medicine even if you feel better sooner. Stopping too early can cause the infection to come back and may make it harder to treat next time.
special_populations: Older adults (over 60 years old): You may have a higher risk of tendon problems, especially if you also take steroids (like prednisone). Talk to your doctor before doing heavy physical activity. Kidney problems: Your dose may need to be adjusted if your kidneys do not work well. Make sure your doctor knows about any kidney issues. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Levofloxacin is generally not recommended during pregnancy or while nursing unless absolutely necessary. Children: Levofloxacin is generally not recommended for children and teenagers under 18 years old unless specifically prescribed by a doctor for special situations, as it may affect bone and joint development.
